data.title: User Enumeration
data.summary: The application responded differently depending on whether an account existed, allowing valid usernames and email addresses to be confirmed in bulk. A confirmed list of accounts is the input to password spraying and to targeted phishing.
data.description:
Enumeration arises wherever the application is helpful about accounts: a login that distinguishes "unknown user" from "wrong password", a reset form that confirms whether an address is registered, a registration form that reports the address as taken, or a response that is simply measurably faster when no password hash is computed.

On its own the impact is limited. Its significance is as the first stage of the attacks that follow — spraying against a known-valid list, and phishing that addresses a real person at a real account.

Timing differences deserve particular attention, because applications that return identical messages often still skip the password hashing step for an unknown user, leaving a difference that is easy to measure.
data.recommendation:
* Return identical responses, with identical timing, whether or not the account exists — including from password reset and registration.
* Perform the password hashing work even for unknown accounts so the response time does not differ.
* Send reset instructions by email in all cases, telling the recipient no account exists where that is so.
* Rate limit the endpoints to make bulk enumeration impractical.
data.short_recommendation: Make authentication responses identical regardless of account.
